opus-5.5.text:
I think the main thing is training models to do harder tasks that unfold over longer horizons. Right now most of the training data, and most of the RL, is on fairly short interactions: you get a prompt, you produce a response, maybe a few turns. So the models are pretty good at things that take a human a few minutes. But when you string together lots of steps, small errors compound and the model doesn't recover well.

Once you start doing reinforcement learning on long tasks, like writing and debugging a whole program, running experiments, or working through a multi-step research problem, I expect the models to get much more coherent over long stretches. A lot of what's missing isn't raw intelligence; it's the ability to notice when something has gone wrong, back up, try a different approach, and keep track of the overall goal. Those are behaviors you can train for once the training episodes are long enough that they matter.

There's also some generalization I'd expect. Pretraining gives you a model that can imitate lots of different kinds of reasoning, and a relatively small amount of long-horizon RL might unlock a lot, because the model already has many of the component skills. It just hasn't been trained to deploy them in a sustained, goal-directed way.

That said, there may be other bottlenecks we haven't hit yet. Memory and context, or certain kinds of judgment that are hard to get reward signals for. So I wouldn't be surprised if long-horizon training gets us a long way but leaves some weaknesses that need separate fixes. My guess is that over the next year or two we'll see models go from mostly helping with individual pieces of a task to carrying out whole projects with much less supervision.

r001.rationale: It says most training data and RL involve short interactions, while long tasks require stringing together many steps.

r002.rationale: It predicts long-task reinforcement learning will make models more coherent over long stretches and better able to carry out whole projects.

r003.rationale: It describes training models to recover when something goes wrong, but does not predict that more capable models will need fewer training examples to learn that behavior.

r004.rationale: It says pretraining supplies component skills that long-horizon RL can unlock, but does not connect generalization from those skills to recovering when a project goes off track.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing holding models back on long projects right now isn't really raw intelligence. If you look at what a model can do in a single step, it's often quite impressive. The problem is that when you chain a lot of steps together, errors compound. You make a small mistake early on, you don't notice it, and then everything downstream is built on a bad foundation. A person doing a long project is constantly checking their work, noticing when something feels off, backing up, and trying a different approach. Models have historically been pretty bad at that kind of self-correction.

So I think a lot of the progress is going to come from training on longer-horizon tasks directly. Right now, most of the RL that gets done is on fairly short episodes, where you get a reward after a few hundred or a few thousand tokens. If you want models to be good at projects that take hours or days, you need to actually train them in that regime, where they have to manage their own context, keep track of what they've tried, and recover from mistakes. That's expensive, and it's harder to get a clean reward signal, but I think it's the main lever.

The other piece is that the model needs to get better at knowing what it doesn't know. A lot of failures on long tasks are the model being confidently wrong about some intermediate result, and then never revisiting it. If you can get the model to be well-calibrated about its uncertainty, it'll naturally spend more effort verifying the parts that are shaky, and that makes the whole thing much more robust.

And then there's the boring infrastructure stuff. Better tools, better ways to store and retrieve information, letting the model actually run tests and look at the results rather than guessing. Humans doing long projects lean heavily on external memory and tools, and I think models will too. So some of what looks like "the model got smarter" will actually be "the model got a better environment to work in."

I'd expect this to improve fairly steadily. I don't think there's one trick. It's going to be a combination of training on longer tasks, better calibration, and better scaffolding, and each of those compounds with the others.

r002.rationale: It predicts that training on longer-horizon tasks is the main lever for making models better at projects lasting hours or days.

r003.rationale: It does not say more capable models will need fewer training examples to learn recovery.

r004.rationale: It does not identify generalization from other abilities as a way to recover when a project goes off track.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it will be training on tasks that actually require a long time to complete. If you mostly train a model on questions it can answer in a few seconds, you’re not putting much pressure on it to develop the skills needed for a project that takes hours or days.

For those projects, it has to keep track of what it’s trying to accomplish, check whether it’s making progress, and recover when an approach doesn’t work. Even if each individual action is pretty reliable, mistakes accumulate over a long sequence. So you need the model to notice mistakes and correct them, rather than requiring every step to be right the first time.

The tricky part is getting a useful training signal. With coding, you can sometimes run tests and see whether the result works. With a more open-ended project, it’s harder to tell whether the model did a good job. And if you only get feedback after several hours, that makes experimentation and learning slower.

So I’d expect progress to come from a combination of better models and better ways of training and evaluating these longer interactions. You can get some improvement by giving the model tools and a place to keep notes, but ultimately it needs practice doing the whole thing.

r002.rationale: It predicts that training on tasks requiring a long time will help models develop the skills needed to carry out long projects.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that more capable models will need fewer examples to learn recovery.

r004.rationale: It discusses noticing and correcting mistakes but does not identify generalization from other abilities as a way to recover.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it will come from training on longer tasks, where the model has to do some work, see what happened, and then keep going. Right now, a lot of training is focused on producing a good answer in a relatively short interaction. That doesn’t necessarily teach you how to make steady progress over a project that takes days.

For a long project, you need to keep track of what you’ve tried, notice when an approach isn’t working, and decide when to step back and revise the plan. You also need to check your work. Otherwise, a small mistake early on can send you down the wrong path for a long time.

So I’d expect progress from a combination of reinforcement learning on longer tasks and better ways of managing the model’s context and recording intermediate results. The hard part is getting useful feedback. With coding, you can run tests, although passing the tests isn’t always the same as solving the actual problem. For more open-ended projects, judging whether you’re making progress is harder.

I don’t think we know yet how much of this will require new ideas versus scaling up methods we already have. But training models in settings where they actually have to recover from mistakes seems pretty important.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts short interactions with long projects, but does not clearly say that most training data concerns individual steps.

r002.rationale: It predicts that training on longer tasks, including through reinforcement learning, will drive much of the progress on long projects.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that more capable models will need fewer examples to learn recovery.

r004.rationale: It does not identify generalization from other abilities as a way to recover when a project goes off track.
